questions.title: Find the Head of a Live Blocking Chain
questions.prompt: Users are reporting the application is frozen. You suspect blocking, not an outage. Write the T-SQL you'd run right now against the live server to find the head blocker — the session that isn't waiting on anyone else but is blocking everyone downstream — and explain what you'd do with the session ID once you have it.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests joined to sys.dm_exec_sessions, filtering for sessions that have a non-zero blocking_session_id to see everyone currently blocked, then specifically look for the blocking_session_id value that does not itself appear as a session_id with its own non-zero blocking_session_id — that session is the head blocker, the one actually holding the lock everyone else is waiting on. Once I have it, I'd pull its current or last statement via sys.dm_exec_sql_text and check open_tran_count and last_request_start_time to understand what it's actually doing and how long it's been doing it, rather than acting blind. Only if it's clearly stuck or abnormally long-running would I consider KILLing the session, understanding that the kill itself rolls back its transaction and can take as long or longer than letting it finish. The real fix afterward is to find out why that session held locks so long — a missing index causing a slow scan while holding a write lock, or application code that doesn't commit promptly — because KILL is an emergency release valve, not a repeatable procedure.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I hear 'the app is frozen,' my first move is never to panic and start killing sessions — it's to find out if this is actually blocking, and if so, where it starts. I'd run a query against dm_exec_requests joined to dm_exec_sessions, filtering for anyone currently blocked, and then specifically look for the one session that's blocking others but isn't itself waiting on anyone — that's my head blocker. Before I touch it, I want to know what it's actually running and how long it's been running it, because killing it rolls back its transaction, and that rollback can take just as long as letting it finish. Once things are stable again, the real work starts: finding out why that session held locks that long in the first place, because if I don't fix that, I'm back here again next week.
questions.example:
SELECT 
    r.session_id,
    r.blocking_session_id,
    r.wait_type,
    r.wait_time,
    r.status,
    s.login_name,
    s.host_name,
    t.text AS running_sql
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests AS r
JOIN sys.dm_exec_sessions AS s ON s.session_id = r.session_id
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) AS t
WHERE r.session_id IN (
    SELECT blocking_session_id FROM sys.dm_exec_requests WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0
)
AND r.blocking_session_id = 0;  -- the head blocker: blocking others, blocked by no one
commonMistakes: Immediately KILLs a session without identifying the actual head blocker first
Confuses a long-running query with a blocking chain — not every slow query is blocking others
Doesn't capture what the head blocker's own transaction was doing before acting
Treats sp_who2 output alone as sufficient without the actual SQL text or wait info
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the head-blocker query pattern using DMVs
Explains the difference between being blocked and being the source of blocking
Describes a safe escalation path (investigate before KILL)
Connects the fix back to root cause (missing index, long transaction, app behavior)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working query identifying the head blocker
Explains the DMV logic clearly
Describes a safe, sensible escalation/response procedure
Connects to durable root-cause fix, not just killing sessions

questions.title: Replace a Row-by-Row Price Update With a Set-Based Rewrite
questions.prompt: A nightly job uses a cursor to apply a different percentage increase to ListPrice per product category, reading category-specific rates from a rates table. It takes 40 minutes against 2 million products. Rewrite it as a single set-based statement.
questions.modelAnswer: The cursor's cost comes from processing one row at a time — a fetch, a lookup, and an update per product, each with its own overhead, multiplied by two million. SQL Server's storage engine is built to process sets of rows efficiently, so the fix is to express the same logic as a single UPDATE joined to the rates table, letting the engine apply the whole operation at once instead of looping. I'd use ISNULL to handle any product whose subcategory has no matching rate, so it's left unchanged rather than silently zeroed out by a NULL multiplication. I'd check that the join column is indexed before declaring victory, and only consider batching the update (e.g., with TOP(n) in a loop) if the single statement itself causes problematic lock duration or transaction log growth at this volume — I wouldn't reach for batching as the first move.
questions.professionalAnswer: Forty minutes for two million rows is a huge tell that something's being processed one row at a time, and sure enough, that's exactly what the cursor is doing — a fetch, a lookup, and an update per product, over and over. My rewrite is a single UPDATE joined to the rates table, because that lets the storage engine do what it's actually built for, which is operating on a whole set at once instead of looping. The one detail I wouldn't skip is handling products whose subcategory has no matching rate — I use a LEFT JOIN with ISNULL so those rows just stay unchanged instead of silently getting multiplied by a NULL. And I'd check the join column has an index before I call this done, because a 40-minute cursor sometimes hides a missing index underneath it too.
commonMistakes: Keeps per-row logic inside a WHILE loop over a temp table, which is just a hand-rolled cursor
Forgets to handle categories with no matching rate row (NULL rate silently zeroing the increase)
Doesn't check whether the join column is indexed before declaring victory
Jumps to batching/chunking as the first solution instead of trying the plain set-based statement first
keyPoints: Correctly diagnoses the cursor as the core bottleneck, not server hardware
Produces a correct, equivalent set-based UPDATE...FROM
Handles the no-matching-rate case correctly (ISNULL or join behavior)
Considers indexing and batching only as secondary, scale-driven refinements

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses cursor overhead as root cause
Produces a correct, working set-based rewrite
Handles edge cases (no matching rate) correctly
Discusses sensible secondary considerations (indexing, batching) without over-engineering

questions.title: Write a tiered customer-value measure with VAR and ALLEXCEPT
questions.prompt: Write a DAX measure against FactInternetSales/DimCustomer that classifies every customer into 'Platinum' (>= $50,000 lifetime revenue), 'Gold' (>= $10,000), or 'Standard,' usable both as a calculated column and referenced from report-level measures. Use VAR to avoid double evaluation, and explain why ALLEXCEPT rather than a plain CALCULATE filter is required for this to work correctly inside a calculated column.
questions.modelAnswer: The measure needs CALCULATE with ALLEXCEPT, not a bare SUM, because this expression lives inside row context (a calculated column, one row per customer) and must be converted into a filter scoped to that one customer before SUM(FactInternetSales[SalesAmount]) means anything company-wide-safe. Referencing CALCULATE inside row context triggers context transition: the current row (one CustomerKey) becomes a one-row filter on DimCustomer. ALLEXCEPT(DimCustomer, DimCustomer[CustomerKey]) then strips every other filter that might already be active on DimCustomer while deliberately preserving the one context transition just created on CustomerKey — so the SUM aggregates exactly that customer's full sales history, regardless of what other DimCustomer filters happen to be active elsewhere in the model at evaluation time. A plain CALCULATE(SUM(...), DimCustomer[CustomerKey] = EARLIER(...)) approach is fragile and non-idiomatic; ALLEXCEPT is the standard, maintainable pattern here. VAR computes CustomerRevenue once and reuses it across all three SWITCH branches instead of re-evaluating the same CALCULATE three times, which matters because this runs once per customer row — on a model with hundreds of thousands of customers, tripling that CALCULATE cost is a real, measurable performance hit, not a style nitpick.
questions.professionalAnswer: My approach here is: compute the number once, then branch on it. I wrap SUM in CALCULATE with ALLEXCEPT on CustomerKey, because this is going into a calculated column, which means I'm in row context — one customer at a time — and I need that row context converted into a filter scoped to just this customer before SUM means anything safe. ALLEXCEPT is what lets me say 'clear every other filter on this table, but keep the one tied to the current customer' — that's exactly the context-transition pattern. Then I stash that in a VAR and SWITCH on it three times instead of calling CALCULATE three separate times — on a customer table with real volume, that's not a style choice, it's cutting the evaluation cost by two-thirds. I'd also mention: if this needs to work as a report-level measure too, not just a calculated column, the same VAR/CALCULATE/ALLEXCEPT shape works fine either way, because CALCULATE's context-transition behavior triggers the same way whether the row context comes from a calculated column or from a measure being evaluated inside an iterator.
questions.example:
Customer Value Tier =
VAR CustomerRevenue =
    CALCULATE(
        SUM(FactInternetSales[SalesAmount]),
        ALLEXCEPT(DimCustomer, DimCustomer[CustomerKey])
    )
RETURN
    SWITCH(
        TRUE(),
        CustomerRevenue >= 50000, "Platinum",
        CustomerRevenue >= 10000, "Gold",
        "Standard"
    )
commonMistakes: Using a plain SUM with no CALCULATE, producing a grand total instead of a per-customer total
Using ALL(DimCustomer) instead of ALLEXCEPT, wiping out the context-transition filter entirely
Calling CALCULATE three separate times instead of once into a VAR
Forgetting that context transition only happens because CALCULATE is explicitly invoked inside row context
keyPoints: Calculated columns run in row context; CALCULATE inside row context triggers context transition
ALLEXCEPT preserves the context-transition filter while clearing other filters on the table
VAR avoids repeating an expensive CALCULATE across multiple SWITCH branches
SWITCH(TRUE(), ...) is the idiomatic tiered-threshold pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Produces correct, working DAX using VAR and ALLEXCEPT
Correctly explains why ALLEXCEPT (not ALL or a bare filter) is required
Explains the context-transition mechanism accurately
Justifies VAR as a performance improvement, not just a style preference

questions.title: Build a dynamic RLS role with a bidirectional mapping table
questions.prompt: Design and write a dynamic RLS role for a model where a ManagerTerritoryMap table (ManagerUPN, TerritoryID) sits on the 'one' side of a relationship to DimSalesTerritory, which itself relates to FactInternetSales. A manager should see only sales for their assigned territory. Write the role expression, specify exactly which relationship setting needs to change and why, and state the one constraint that setting is subject to.
questions.modelAnswer: The role itself is a single dynamic filter on the mapping table: [ManagerUPN] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(). The problem is relationship direction: by default an RLS filter only flows one way across a relationship regardless of the relationship's own cross-filter direction setting, and ManagerTerritoryMap sits on the side that needs the filter to flow outward — through DimSalesTerritory and on to FactInternetSales — not just filter itself. Left at the default, the filter on ManagerTerritoryMap would narrow that table down to the signed-in manager's row but never propagate out to actually restrict which FactInternetSales rows are visible. The fix is enabling 'Apply security filter in both directions' on the relationship between ManagerTerritoryMap and DimSalesTerritory, which lets the RLS filter — specifically, and only the RLS filter, not ordinary report filtering — flow in both directions across that relationship. The constraint to flag before enabling it: if DimSalesTerritory (or whichever table sits in the middle) already participates in more than one bidirectional relationship, this option can only be enabled on one of them — you can't bidirectionally-filter-for-security on two relationships touching the same table simultaneously. It's also worth validating with Test as role before trusting it, and testing for a real performance regression, since bidirectional security filtering has a genuine query-time cost on a large fact table like FactInternetSales.
questions.professionalAnswer: The role expression itself is simple — ManagerUPN equals USERPRINCIPALNAME() on the mapping table. The real work is getting the filter to actually reach FactInternetSales, because by default RLS filters are one-directional regardless of how the relationship's normal cross-filtering is configured. Since my mapping table sits upstream of DimSalesTerritory, I need to turn on 'Apply security filter in both directions' on that specific relationship — that's the one setting that lets the security filter, specifically, propagate the direction I need. The thing I always check before flipping that switch: does DimSalesTerritory already have another bidirectional relationship elsewhere in the model? Because if it does, I can only enable this option on one of them — Power BI won't let me stack it. After that, I validate with Test as role and I genuinely load-test it, because bidirectional security filtering isn't free — on a fact table this size it can show up as real query latency, and 'technically correct but three seconds slower' isn't a result I'd ship without flagging it first.
commonMistakes: Writing the role expression but leaving the relationship as single-directional, so the filter never reaches the fact table
Enabling bidirectional security filtering on every relationship touching the table instead of checking the one-per-table constraint
Not load-testing the performance cost before deploying
Confusing bidirectional security filtering with ordinary bidirectional cross-filtering (a different, unrelated setting)
keyPoints: Dynamic RLS role expression: [ManagerUPN] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
RLS filters are single-directional by default regardless of relationship cross-filter mode
Apply security filter in both directions propagates the RLS filter specifically
A table can only have this setting enabled on one of its relationships if it has multiple bidirectional ones
Performance cost must be tested, especially on large fact tables

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct dynamic RLS role expression
Correctly identifies the need for bidirectional security filtering and why
States the one-relationship-per-table constraint accurately
Mentions validation (Test as role) and performance cost

questions.title: Write a Running 12-Month Total and Month-over-Month Delta for a BI Semantic View
questions.prompt: A reporting view, MonthlySales(StoreId, SalesMonth, SalesAmount), feeds a Power BI DirectQuery dashboard. The dashboard team wants two new columns computed in the view itself (to keep the model thin): a trailing 12-month rolling total per store, and the month-over-month dollar change per store. Write the T-SQL using window functions, partitioned correctly per store and ordered by month.
questions.modelAnswer: Both columns are windowed aggregates partitioned by StoreId and ordered by SalesMonth, but they need different frame/function choices. The rolling 12-month total uses SUM(SalesAmount) OVER (PARTITION BY StoreId ORDER BY SalesMonth ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) — ROWS BETWEEN, not RANGE, is deliberate: ROWS counts physical rows (12 monthly rows including the current one), while RANGE would group by value ties on SalesMonth, which isn't the intent here. The month-over-month delta uses LAG(SalesAmount, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY StoreId ORDER BY SalesMonth) to pull the prior month's value into the same row, then subtracts it from the current SalesAmount; the first month per store correctly returns NULL since there's no prior month to compare against, which is the right behavior rather than something to coalesce away. One real gotcha: if a store has a gap month with no row at all (zero sales recorded as a missing row rather than a zero row), the rolling total silently covers fewer than 12 calendar months and the MoM delta compares against the wrong month — that assumes one row exists per store per calendar month, which should be validated against the actual data before shipping this.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this as a single SELECT with two window functions, both partitioned by StoreId so one store's numbers never bleed into another's, and both ordered by SalesMonth since that's what 'trailing' and 'month-over-month' are relative to. For the rolling 12-month total, I'd use SUM(SalesAmount) OVER (PARTITION BY StoreId ORDER BY SalesMonth ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) — I'd specifically call out ROWS instead of RANGE, because ROWS gives me a fixed window of 12 physical rows, whereas RANGE would behave oddly if there were ever duplicate month values. For month-over-month, LAG is the natural fit: LAG(SalesAmount) OVER (PARTITION BY StoreId ORDER BY SalesMonth) grabs last month's value onto the current row so I can just subtract. I'd leave the first row per store as NULL rather than coalescing it to zero, since there genuinely isn't a prior month to compare against and that's a meaningful distinction for the dashboard. Before calling this done, I'd ask whether every store has exactly one row per calendar month with no gaps — if a month is just missing instead of zero, both the rolling total and the MoM comparison quietly go wrong, and that's worth checking against the real table before trusting the output.
questions.example:
SELECT
    StoreId,
    SalesMonth,
    SalesAmount,
    SUM(SalesAmount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY StoreId
        ORDER BY SalesMonth
        ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS Rolling12MonthTotal,
    SalesAmount - LAG(SalesAmount, 1) OVER (
        PARTITION BY StoreId
        ORDER BY SalesMonth
    ) AS MonthOverMonthDelta
FROM MonthlySales
ORDER BY StoreId, SalesMonth;
commonMistakes: Using RANGE BETWEEN instead of ROWS BETWEEN for the rolling window, which behaves incorrectly with duplicate or tied order-by values
Omitting PARTITION BY StoreId, causing the rolling total and LAG to blend data across different stores
Coalescing the first-row NULL from LAG to zero, masking the fact that no prior month exists for comparison
Not validating that each store has exactly one row per calendar month, which silently breaks both the rolling total and the MoM delta if months are missing
Using a self-join or correlated subquery instead of window functions, which is far slower and harder to maintain
keyPoints: PARTITION BY StoreId keeps both window calculations scoped per store
ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW gives a fixed 12-row rolling window, distinct from RANGE semantics
LAG(SalesAmount, 1) retrieves the prior month's value for the month-over-month subtraction
The first row per store legitimately returns NULL for the MoM delta and should not be coalesced
Correctness depends on one row existing per store per calendar month with no gaps

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct PARTITION BY/ORDER BY on both window functions
Correct use of ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (not RANGE)
Correct LAG-based month-over-month delta calculation
Identifies the gap-month / missing-row data assumption risk

questions.title: Generate One DAG Per Client From a Shared Config File
questions.prompt: Instead of hand-writing a near-identical DAG for each of 12 clients' nightly loads, write an Airflow DAG-generation script that reads a local JSON config file and produces one DAG per client, each with its own schedule and a single PythonOperator task.
questions.code:
import json
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import datetime

from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator

CONFIG_PATH = Path(__file__).parent / "client_configs.json"
CLIENT_CONFIGS = json.loads(CONFIG_PATH.read_text())


def load_client_data(client_id: str, **context):
    print(f"Loading nightly data for client {client_id}")
    # real extraction/load logic goes here


def build_client_dag(client_id: str, schedule: str) -> DAG:
    with DAG(
        dag_id=f"client_load_{client_id}",
        schedule_interval=schedule,
        start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
        catchup=False,
        tags=["client-load", client_id],
    ) as dag:
        PythonOperator(
            task_id="load_client_data",
            python_callable=load_client_data,
            op_kwargs={"client_id": client_id},
        )
    return dag


for config in CLIENT_CONFIGS:
    dag_id = f"client_load_{config['client_id']}"
    globals()[dag_id] = build_client_dag(config["client_id"], config["schedule"])
questions.modelAnswer: The config (client_configs.json) is read from a local file at module import/parse time, kept deliberately cheap rather than a live database or API call, which matters because the scheduler re-parses this file on every parse interval and a slow config read would be paid repeatedly. build_client_dag constructs a distinct DAG object per client with its own dag_id and schedule; the critical step most people get wrong is the final loop assigning each built DAG to globals()[dag_id] -- Airflow's DAG file processor only picks up DAG objects that exist in the module's global namespace, so building DAGs inside a function and returning them without this assignment means Airflow never actually discovers them as separate DAGs. Each DAG gets a unique dag_id derived from the client identifier so they're independently visible, schedulable, and pausable in the UI, and tags make them filterable as a group without being a single combined DAG.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through the two things people usually get wrong here: first, the config has to be fast and local -- if this read a live table instead of a JSON file, we'd be adding that query's latency to every scheduler parse cycle for every one of these DAGs, which is the kind of thing that looks fine with 12 clients and becomes a scheduler-health problem at 200. Second, that globals()[dag_id] = build_client_dag(...) line isn't cosmetic -- without it, these DAG objects exist in memory when the file is parsed but Airflow's DAG file processor never registers them, so you'd see zero DAGs in the UI despite the code running without errors. I'd add onboarding a new client to this as just appending one entry to the JSON file and letting the next scheduler parse pick it up automatically.
commonMistakes: Builds DAG objects in a function but never assigns them to the module's global namespace, so Airflow never discovers them
Reads configuration from a live database/API call at parse time instead of a fast local file
Gives every generated DAG the same dag_id or doesn't derive it from the client identifier, causing collisions
Forgets catchup=False, risking a backfill storm across 12 DAGs on first deploy
keyPoints: Reads config from a fast, local source rather than a live query at parse time
Builds a distinct DAG object per client with a unique dag_id and its own schedule
Assigns each generated DAG to the module's global namespace so Airflow discovers it
Sets catchup=False and reasonable defaults to avoid an unintended backfill on rollout

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct DAG-generation loop producing one DAG per config entry
Correctly assigns generated DAGs to globals() so Airflow discovers them
Unique dag_id per client, config read from a fast local source
Explains the scheduler re-parsing implication clearly

questions.title: Dynamically Map a Task Over a Variable-Length List of Files
questions.prompt: A DAG needs to process however many files land in a staging folder each night -- sometimes 3, sometimes 30 -- without hand-writing a task per file or hardcoding a maximum count. Write the Airflow code using dynamic task mapping (.expand()) to fan out a processing task over that list.
questions.modelAnswer: list_staged_files runs once and returns however many filenames actually exist that night; process_file.expand(filename=files) is where the dynamic mapping happens -- Airflow creates one mapped task instance of process_file per element in that list at runtime, not at DAG-parse time, so the count genuinely varies night to night without any DAG code change or hardcoded maximum. Each mapped instance runs independently (and can retry independently, which matters if file 7 of 30 fails and the others succeeded), and summarize(results) automatically receives the full list of all mapped task outputs by depending on the expand() call's result, giving a single aggregation point after however many instances ran. This is distinct from writing a static for loop over files at DAG-definition time, which can't react to a count that isn't known until the DAG actually runs.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the key distinction as 'known at parse time vs. known at run time' -- a plain for loop in the DAG file has to know the file count when Airflow parses the DAG, which it can't, since that count depends on what lands overnight. Dynamic task mapping defers that decision to execution time: list_staged_files runs, returns whatever it finds, and .expand() creates exactly that many task instances, each independently retryable, so one bad file doesn't take down the other 29. I'd also point out that summarize() depending on the expand() output is what gives us a clean single place to roll up a pass/fail report, instead of needing a separate join step.
commonMistakes: Writes a static Python for loop over files at DAG-definition time instead of using .expand()
Doesn't realize each mapped task instance can retry independently, treating the whole expand() as one atomic unit
Forgets to have a downstream task depend on the expand() result to aggregate/summarize outcomes
Hardcodes an assumed maximum file count instead of letting the list determine fan-out size at runtime
keyPoints: Uses .expand() to fan out a task over a runtime-determined list
Understands expansion happens at execution time, not DAG-parse time
Notes each mapped instance retries independently
Aggregates mapped results in a downstream task depending on the expand() output

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct use of .expand() for dynamic task mapping
Correctly explains parse-time vs. run-time determination of fan-out count
Includes a sensible downstream aggregation step
Notes independent retry behavior of mapped instances

questions.title: Convert a Polling File Sensor to a Deferrable Sensor
questions.prompt: A DAG uses a standard poke-mode S3KeySensor with a 5-minute poke interval and a 6-hour timeout, tying up a worker slot the entire time it waits. Rewrite it to use the deferrable equivalent so it releases the worker slot while waiting.
questions.code:
# Before: ties up a worker slot for up to 6 hours
# from airflow.providers.amazon.aws.sensors.s3 import S3KeySensor
# wait_for_file = S3KeySensor(
#     task_id="wait_for_file",
#     bucket_name="client-staging",
#     bucket_key="nightly/{{ ds }}/extract.csv",
#     poke_interval=300,
#     timeout=60 * 60 * 6,
# )

# After: defers to the triggerer, releases the worker slot while waiting
from airflow.providers.amazon.aws.sensors.s3 import S3KeySensor

wait_for_file = S3KeySensor(
    task_id="wait_for_file",
    bucket_name="client-staging",
    bucket_key="nightly/{{ ds }}/extract.csv",
    poke_interval=300,
    timeout=60 * 60 * 6,
    deferrable=True,
)
questions.modelAnswer: Setting deferrable=True on a sensor that supports it (most AWS/GCP provider sensors do) changes its execution model without changing any of its matching logic: instead of occupying a worker slot and sleeping between pokes, the task runs an initial check, and if the condition isn't met yet, it defers -- handing the wait off to the triggerer process as an async trigger and fully releasing its worker slot -- then only resumes on a worker when the triggerer notifies it the file has arrived or the timeout is reached. The poke_interval and timeout semantics are preserved (the triggerer uses them to pace its async checks and enforce the same deadline); the only operational change is that during the wait, this task consumes no worker slot at all, just a lightweight entry in the triggerer, which matters a lot once you have many of these running concurrently. The prerequisite that's easy to forget is that an Airflow triggerer process has to actually be running in the deployment for deferrable=True to work -- without it, the task will be stuck unable to resume.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a one-line change on the task, but I'd flag to the team that it only works if we're actually running a triggerer component in this deployment -- if we're on a setup that's never needed one before, this is also an infrastructure change, not just a code change. Once that's confirmed, deferrable=True is close to a free win here: same timeout, same poke cadence from the user's perspective, but the worker slot that used to be pinned for up to 6 hours is now free for other DAGs almost the entire time we're waiting. I'd roll this out to our other long-polling sensors too once we've confirmed it works cleanly on this one.
commonMistakes: Assumes deferrable=True works without a triggerer process actually running in the deployment
Changes poke_interval or timeout semantics unnecessarily instead of just adding the deferrable flag
Confuses deferrable sensors with reducing the actual wait time, rather than just the worker-slot cost of waiting
Applies deferrable=True to a sensor/operator that doesn't actually support it
keyPoints: Adds deferrable=True to the existing sensor with matching logic unchanged
Explains that this releases the worker slot during the wait instead of blocking it
Notes the triggerer process must be running for this to function
Understands poke_interval/timeout semantics are preserved under deferred execution

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct minimal code change (deferrable=True) preserving existing sensor logic
Correctly explains the worker-slot release mechanism via the triggerer
Notes the triggerer-must-be-running prerequisite
Clear framing of the operational benefit at scale

questions.title: Define a dbt Semantic Layer Metric for a KPI Used by Two BI Tools
questions.prompt: Finance and Sales both want to query 'net_revenue' -- gross revenue minus refunds -- sliced by region and month, from Power BI and from an ad hoc notebook, and they need to get the same number every time. Write the dbt semantic model and metric definitions that make this possible.
questions.code:
# models/semantic/fct_orders.yml
semantic_models:
  - name: fct_orders
    model: ref('fct_orders')
    defaults:
      agg_time_dimension: order_date
    entities:
      - name: order_id
        type: primary
    dimensions:
      - name: order_date
        type: time
        type_params:
          time_granularity: day
      - name: region
        type: categorical
    measures:
      - name: gross_revenue
        agg: sum
        expr: order_total
      - name: refund_amount
        agg: sum
        expr: refund_total

metrics:
  - name: net_revenue
    label: Net Revenue
    type: derived
    type_params:
      expr: gross_revenue - refund_amount
      metrics:
        - name: gross_revenue
        - name: refund_amount
questions.modelAnswer: The semantic model declares fct_orders' entity (order_id), its dimensions (region as categorical, order_date as the time dimension for aggregation), and two base measures (gross_revenue, refund_amount), each tied to a specific column and aggregation. net_revenue is defined as a derived metric -- a formula over two other metrics (here, gross_revenue and refund_amount referenced implicitly as simple metrics over their measures) rather than a new raw aggregation, so the business logic 'net revenue = gross minus refunds' lives in exactly one place. Any consumer asking the Semantic Layer for net_revenue by region and month gets SQL generated from this single definition regardless of whether the request comes from Power BI's Semantic Layer connector or an ad hoc call to the Semantic Layer API from a notebook, which is what actually guarantees Finance and Sales see the same number -- not because they're disciplined, but because there's only one place the subtraction can be defined.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this as one semantic model with two base measures and a derived metric on top, specifically so the subtraction -- gross minus refunds -- exists in exactly one place in the codebase. The part I'd emphasize to Finance and Sales is that this only solves their problem if both tools actually query through the Semantic Layer rather than hitting the underlying table directly; I'd ask both teams to confirm their existing reports get migrated to pull from this metric, not just that new reports use it, otherwise we'll have this same 'three different numbers' conversation again in six months with one of the old reports as the outlier.
commonMistakes: Defines net_revenue as a brand-new raw aggregation instead of a derived metric over existing measures, duplicating logic
Forgets agg_time_dimension, which MetricFlow needs to know how to aggregate the measures over time
Doesn't declare region as a dimension, so slicing by region isn't possible through the Semantic Layer
Assumes defining the metric automatically migrates existing reports off direct table queries
keyPoints: Declares a semantic model with entity, time dimension, categorical dimension, and base measures
Defines net_revenue as a derived metric combining two base metrics rather than a new raw aggregation
Explains why a single definition guarantees consistency across BI tools and notebooks
Flags that existing reports must actually migrate to query through the Semantic Layer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct semantic model YAML (entity, dimensions, measures)
Correct derived metric definition for net_revenue
Clear explanation of why this guarantees cross-tool consistency
Flags the migration/adoption precondition

questions.title: Write a Snowflake-Safe Incremental dbt Model Using merge
questions.prompt: A fct_subscriptions model has 2 billion rows and only needs to process rows changed since the last run, using Snowflake's MERGE-based incremental strategy, keyed on subscription_id, with a lookback window to safely catch late-arriving updates.
questions.modelAnswer: incremental_strategy='merge' tells dbt to generate a MERGE statement on this run that matches incoming rows to existing rows by unique_key (subscription_id) -- updating matched rows and inserting unmatched ones -- rather than deleting and reinserting or blindly appending, which keeps the operation idempotent even if the same source row appears in two consecutive incremental runs. The is_incremental() block limits the scanned source rows to those with updated_at at or after six hours before the max updated_at already in the target table ({{ this }}), rather than naively filtering by 'since last run time' -- the six-hour lookback is the safety margin against late-arriving updates (a row that gets updated in the source system slightly after the last run's cutoff but with a timestamp that technically fell before it, due to clock skew or batched upstream writes) being missed entirely by a tighter window. cluster_by on updated_at helps because this table is queried and filtered by recency far more than by any other column, improving pruning on both the incremental read and downstream analytical queries.
questions.professionalAnswer: The two things I'd walk an interviewer through: why MERGE and why the lookback. MERGE is the right strategy here because subscription status genuinely gets updated in place -- a row doesn't just get appended, its status can flip from active to canceled -- so a strategy that can't update existing rows (like plain append) would leave the table permanently out of date for anyone whose subscription changed after their first row landed. The lookback window exists because 'only rows since the last successful run' sounds safe but isn't, in practice, once you've been burned once by a late-arriving update landing in the source system with a timestamp just before the cutoff and never getting picked up -- six hours of overlap costs a little extra scan, which is a much cheaper mistake than silently missing updates forever.
commonMistakes: Uses incremental_strategy='append' for data that actually gets updated in place, silently going stale for updated rows
Filters strictly by a 'since last run' timestamp with no lookback window, missing late-arriving/out-of-order updates
Forgets unique_key, which MERGE requires to know how to match existing rows
Doesn't use {{ this }} to reference the target table's current max watermark inside is_incremental()
keyPoints: Uses incremental_strategy='merge' with a correct unique_key
Implements is_incremental() filtering off {{ this }}'s current max watermark
Includes a deliberate lookback window to catch late-arriving updates
Chooses cluster_by aligned with the actual dominant query/filter pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct incremental config (strategy, unique_key)
Correct is_incremental() logic using {{ this }}
Includes and justifies a lookback window for late-arriving data
Explains why merge (not append) fits this data's update pattern

questions.title: Bringing a Manually Created Event Hub Under Bicep Management
questions.prompt: Six months ago, someone manually provisioned a production Event Hub namespace through the Azure Portal under time pressure. It's never been touched since, but now it needs to go through the same CI/CD-managed Bicep pipeline as everything else. Explain how you'd bring it under IaC management given Bicep/ARM doesn't have a true 'import' command like Terraform, and write the Bicep you'd use.
questions.modelAnswer: Bicep/ARM deployments are declarative and idempotent by name -- there's no separate 'import state' step like terraform import, because ARM doesn't track resource ownership the way Terraform's state file does. 'Importing' in practice means writing a Bicep resource block whose type, name, and properties exactly match the resource's CURRENT live configuration, then deploying it. Because ARM resolves a deployment by matching resource type and name, deploying a Bicep definition that matches an existing resource's current state is effectively a no-op update, and from that point forward the resource is 'under management' in the sense that the next deployment touching this Bicep file will apply diffs to it going forward. The critical risk is capturing the TRUE current configuration before writing that block -- if the manually-created Event Hub has settings (a specific capacity, a non-default retention, a particular throughput configuration) that get guessed wrong in the Bicep definition, the first deployment silently changes production instead of leaving it alone. The existing keyword resource reference is the safe way to read and confirm current properties before writing the managed resource block, rather than guessing. I'd also run a what-if deployment (az deployment group what-if) before the real apply specifically to confirm it reports zero or no-op changes, which is the actual verification that the Bicep definition genuinely matches reality.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd correct is the premise that we're looking for a terraform-import equivalent -- Bicep just doesn't work that way, since ARM doesn't keep a separate state file tracking what it owns. What actually happens is: we write a Bicep resource block that matches this Event Hub's current settings exactly, and the moment we deploy it and it comes back as a no-op, that resource is under management. The part I'd be most careful about is getting 'exactly' right -- I'd use the existing keyword first to read its real current config rather than guess at what someone set six months ago, and then I would not run this against production without a what-if deployment first. If what-if shows anything other than no changes, that's a sign my Bicep doesn't actually match reality yet, and I'd rather find that out from a dry run than from an unintended change to a live Event Hub.
commonMistakes: Assumes Bicep has a terraform import equivalent command and looks for one instead of writing a matching resource definition
Writes the Bicep resource block from assumed/default settings instead of verifying the resource's actual current configuration first
Skips a what-if deployment before the real apply, risking an unintended production change
Uses the existing keyword as if it brings the resource under management, when it's read-only and changes nothing
Doesn't account for properties that are immutable or hard to change needing to match exactly from day one
keyPoints: Explains ARM/Bicep has no stateful import; management starts by matching a resource's current live config in code
Uses the existing keyword to safely read current configuration before writing the managed definition
Verifies the match with a what-if deployment before the real apply
Flags the risk of a mismatched property causing an unintended change to production on first deploy

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why Bicep has no true import and what bringing under management actually means
Correct use of the existing keyword to verify current state safely
Correctly matches the managed resource definition structure
Proposes what-if verification before the real deployment

questions.title: Configure Git Mode and a CI/CD Publish Pipeline for a Data Factory Instance
questions.prompt: A Data Factory instance has been built entirely by clicking in the browser UX with no source control, and the team wants Dev/Test/Prod promotion with pull-request review before anything reaches Test or Prod. Describe the Git configuration needed in Data Factory itself, and write the key snippet of the Azure DevOps YAML pipeline step that deploys the generated ARM template into the Test Data Factory using parameter overrides (so the Test linked service points at Test resources, not Dev's).
questions.code:
Repo layout after Git integration:
  adf_publish branch (auto-generated, holds ARMTemplateForFactory.json + parameters file)
  main / feature branches (collaboration branches, hold the factory's actual resource JSON)
questions.modelAnswer: Data Factory's Git configuration is set under Manage > Git configuration, pointing the Dev factory at a collaboration branch (commonly main or a release branch) in Azure Repos or GitHub. Every change an author makes in the UX is saved to a feature branch and merged into the collaboration branch via pull request, which is what provides the required review gate — nothing reaches the collaboration branch without a PR. Clicking 'Publish' from the collaboration branch is what generates the ARM template and pushes it to the auto-created adf_publish branch; adf_publish is a build artifact, not something anyone edits by hand. The CI/CD pipeline then takes ARMTemplateForFactory.json from adf_publish and deploys it with an ARM/Bicep deployment task, overriding the environment-specific parameters (linked service connection strings, Key Vault references) defined in ARMTemplateParametersForFactory.json so the same template deploys correctly to Test and then Prod without any hard-coded Dev values leaking through.
questions.professionalAnswer: First step, before any pipeline work, is wiring up Git configuration inside the Dev factory itself — under Manage > Git configuration, pointed at a collaboration branch like main. Once that's set, every change someone makes in the ADF UX lands on a feature branch, and getting it into main requires a pull request, which is exactly the review gate the team's asking for — nobody can push straight to the branch that matters. Publishing from that collaboration branch is what generates the ARM template into the auto-managed adf_publish branch; I'd explain that nobody should ever hand-edit adf_publish, it's purely generated output. For the actual promotion pipeline, I'd have the Azure DevOps YAML pull ARMTemplateForFactory.json from adf_publish and run an ARM deployment task against the Test factory's resource group, passing overrideParameters so things like the Test SQL linked service connection string get substituted in instead of whatever was baked in for Dev — the template itself stays identical across environments, only the parameter values change per stage.
questions.example:
# Azure DevOps YAML — deploy ADF ARM template into the Test Data Factory
- task: AzureResourceManagerTemplateDeployment@3
  displayName: 'Deploy ARM Template to Test Data Factory'
  inputs:
    deploymentScope: 'Resource Group'
    azureResourceManagerConnection: 'AzureServiceConnection-Test'
    subscriptionId: '$(testSubscriptionId)'
    action: 'Create Or Update Resource Group'
    resourceGroupName: '$(testResourceGroupName)'
    location: 'East US'
    templateLocation: 'Linked artifact'
    csmFile: '$(Pipeline.Workspace)/adf_publish/ARMTemplateForFactory.json'
    csmParametersFile: '$(Pipeline.Workspace)/adf_publish/ARMTemplateParametersForFactory.json'
    overrideParameters: >
      -factoryName "adf-test-bi"
      -AzureSqlDatabase_connectionString "$(TestSqlConnectionString)"
    deploymentMode: 'Incremental'
commonMistakes: Never configuring Git integration on the Dev factory, leaving all changes unversioned and unreviewable
Manually editing the adf_publish branch instead of treating it strictly as generated publish output
Deploying the same ARM template to Test without overriding environment-specific parameters, pointing Test at Dev's linked services
Using Incremental deployment mode assumptions incorrectly or switching to Complete mode, which can delete resources not present in the template
Allowing direct pushes to the collaboration branch instead of enforcing pull-request review via branch policy
keyPoints: Git configuration is set on the Dev factory, pointing at a collaboration branch with branch-policy-enforced PR review
adf_publish is auto-generated by Publish and should never be hand-edited
ARMTemplateForFactory.json plus its parameters file are the artifacts carried through the release pipeline
overrideParameters substitutes environment-specific values (connection strings, factory name) per stage
Incremental deployment mode is used so the deployment doesn't delete resources outside the template unexpectedly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes Git configuration and PR-gated collaboration branch workflow
Correctly explains adf_publish as generated, not hand-edited
Correct ARM deployment YAML task structure
Correct use of overrideParameters for environment-specific values

lessonLink.label: Review: ARM Templates & Azure DevOps Pipelines

questions.title: Write a Terraform Module for a Reusable, Environment-Parameterized Storage Account
questions.prompt: Three environments (dev, staging, prod) each need a storage account for a data pipeline's landing zone, differing only in naming, redundancy tier, and tags. Write a reusable Terraform module (not copy-pasted per environment) that takes environment as an input and provisions the storage account accordingly.
questions.modelAnswer: The module takes environment as a required, validated input rather than three near-identical hardcoded resource blocks, and derives the environment-specific differences -- naming, replication tier, tags -- from that single input using a local lookup map rather than if/else chains repeated per environment. The validation block rejects anything other than dev/staging/prod at plan time, which catches a typo in the calling code before it ever reaches Azure instead of silently defaulting to something wrong. Each environment's own root module (envs/dev, envs/staging, envs/prod) then has a short, nearly identical block that just calls the module with a different environment value and its own state/backend configuration, so the actual resource logic lives in exactly one place. The replication tier lookup -- LRS for dev/staging, GRS for prod -- demonstrates the real point of a module: environment-specific business rules (prod needs geo-redundancy, lower environments don't need to pay for it) are expressed once, in the module, instead of being re-decided and potentially gotten wrong in three separate copy-pasted files.
questions.professionalAnswer: My rule of thumb is if I'm about to copy-paste a resource block for a second environment, it should already be a module. I'd write the module to take environment as input, validate it so a typo fails fast instead of silently misconfiguring something, and push every environment-specific decision -- naming, replication, tags -- into a lookup inside the module rather than scattering if-statements across three environment folders. The payoff shows up later: when someone asks 'why is prod GRS and dev LRS,' the answer lives in exactly one file, and when a fourth environment shows up, it's one new short caller block, not a fourth copy of the whole resource.
commonMistakes: Copy-pastes near-identical resource blocks per environment instead of writing a parameterized module
Hardcodes environment-specific values (replication tier, naming) without input validation, so a typo in the environment variable silently misconfigures a resource
Puts environment-specific business logic (e.g. prod needs GRS) in the calling code instead of inside the module itself
Doesn't expose module outputs needed by other resources, forcing the caller to hardcode or re-derive values
keyPoints: Single reusable module parameterized by an environment input
Input validation to catch invalid environment values at plan time
Environment-specific differences expressed via a lookup map inside the module, not duplicated resource blocks
Clean module interface (variables in, outputs out) so callers stay thin
Correctly ties the business rule (prod redundancy) to the module's internal logic

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, reusable module structure (variables, main, outputs)
Correct environment-driven parameterization with validation
Keeps environment-specific business logic inside the module, not duplicated in callers
Clean explanation of why this beats copy-paste per environment

questions.title: Build a Resource Monitor That Suspends a Warehouse at 100% and Only Notifies at 75%
questions.prompt: Finance wants warnings at 75% of a monthly compute budget but a hard stop at 100% so a runaway job can't blow through the budget entirely. Write the Snowflake SQL to create a resource monitor enforcing this on a specific warehouse, and explain the difference between the suspend and suspend_immediate actions.
questions.code:
CREATE OR REPLACE RESOURCE MONITOR etl_monthly_budget
  WITH
    CREDIT_QUOTA = 5000
    FREQUENCY = MONTHLY
    START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY
  TRIGGERS
    ON 75 PERCENT DO NOTIFY
    ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND
    ON 110 PERCENT DO SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE;

ALTER WAREHOUSE etl_wh SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = etl_monthly_budget;
questions.modelAnswer: The resource monitor is created with a CREDIT_QUOTA for the budget and MONTHLY FREQUENCY so it resets automatically each billing period, with three triggers at increasing thresholds. The 75 PERCENT NOTIFY trigger only sends an alert to the monitor's configured recipients -- it doesn't stop anything, which is exactly what's wanted for an early warning. The 100 PERCENT SUSPEND trigger lets any currently running queries finish before suspending the warehouse, which protects in-flight work from being killed mid-query but means a single long-running runaway query could still push consumption past 100% while it finishes. SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE, which I added as a safety threshold slightly above 100%, cancels running queries immediately rather than waiting for them to finish -- that's the real hard stop finance is asking for, so I wouldn't rely on the 100% SUSPEND trigger alone if the actual requirement is 'cannot blow through the budget,' since a single bad query finishing could still exceed it under plain SUSPEND. Finally, the monitor is attached to the specific warehouse via ALTER WAREHOUSE ... SET RESOURCE_MONITOR, and note a resource monitor can also be set at the account level, so it's worth confirming this one is scoped to the single warehouse finance actually means.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this in the three tiers finance is describing without them realizing there's a subtlety: a soft warning, a 'please wrap up' suspend, and a true hard stop. The part I'd flag back to finance explicitly is that SUSPEND at 100% is not actually a hard stop -- it lets whatever's running finish first, so if the real requirement is 'this can never exceed budget,' I'd add a SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE trigger just above 100% as the actual enforcement, and set expectations that SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE does cancel in-flight queries, which is a tradeoff they need to sign off on, not something to silently build in.
commonMistakes: Uses only a single 100% SUSPEND trigger and calls it a hard stop, missing that in-flight queries are allowed to finish
Confuses SUSPEND (graceful, lets running queries finish) with SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE (cancels running queries)
Forgets FREQUENCY = MONTHLY, so the quota never resets
Doesn't scope the monitor to the specific warehouse and accidentally applies it account-wide
keyPoints: Correct CREDIT_QUOTA, FREQUENCY, and multi-threshold TRIGGERS syntax
Correctly distinguishes NOTIFY (alert only) from SUSPEND (graceful) from SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE (hard cancel)
Recognizes plain SUSPEND at 100% isn't a true hard stop and proposes a SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE safety threshold
Correctly scopes the monitor to the intended warehouse via ALTER WAREHOUSE

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working resource monitor SQL with multiple thresholds
Correctly explains SUSPEND vs. SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE semantics
Recognizes the gap between 'suspend at 100%' and a true hard stop
Correct warehouse-level scoping
